newsitem.title: MEXICO: YEAREND - Guerrillas, disasters haunted Latin America in 1996.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Guerrillas, disasters haunted Latin America in 1996.

text.p: It was not supposed to be like this.
Guerrillas, poverty and disasters grabbed Latin America's headlines in 1996, reminding the region's emerging economies of a dark past they were doing their best to forget.
Once the darling of foreign investors, Mexico saw the emergence of a new guerrilla group preaching 1970s Marxist ideology and suffered a wave of kidnappings whose victims included market traders.

Chile, the region's economic model, saw its gap between rich and poor yawn even further, and Colombia was officially declared a pariah nation by the United States for failing to do enough to fight drugs.

Billed a few years back as a fast-growing star performer, Argentina's economy fell so far in 1996 that slum-dwellers in one provincial town, Rosario, took to eating pet cats -- not quite what the IMF prescribed.

In a throwback to Cold War days, Cuban warplanes downed two small private U.S. planes in February, saying they had violated its airspace. Washington responded by announcing new sanctions against companies that do business with the island.

Foreign companies were told to comply with the Helms-Burton law or face drastic punishments -- a move that revived old accusations of "gringo imperialism" from Latin American nations long mistrustful of Uncle Sam.

Communist Cuba said it had no intention of changing its one-party system. "In 1959, Cuba began a big political opening that is called revolution, and we are fighting to preserve it and improve it," said Fidel Castro, who turned 70 in August.
AIR DISASTERS

Planes crashed all over Latin America, killing tourists in Guatemala, business people in Sao Paulo, foreigners in Peru and commuters in Colombia. More than 550 people died in eight crashes during 1996 but the nastiest end came to the 189 people aboard a tourist charter flight that crashed into the Caribbean off the Dominican Republic in February -- sharks beat rescuers to the scene.

Peru was particularly unlucky, with two big crashes during the year. Guillermo Arbe, head of Peru research at Morgan Grenfell in Lima, commented: "Memories are short and for many Peruvians daily life is a disaster anyway."

Disaster struck on the ground too. Eighty-one Guatemalans met a particularly gruesome end in October, crushed to death against a chainlink fence in a soccer stadium by an avalanche of bodies as gatecrashers pushed in from above.

Local reaction was muted. This was, after all, a country where more than 140,000 people have been killed in a 35-year civil war -- although the New Year should bring welcome news in the form of a lasting peace agreement between the government and Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) leftist guerrillas.
POLITICAL UNREST

Not so in Colombia, where the country's Marxist-inspired rebels gained strength during 1996. The biggest insurgent force, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), managed to kidnap 60 soldiers and hold them hostage in the country's eastern jungle for more than three months. Army top brass fumed but have so far proved unable to mount a rescue.

Colombian President Ernesto Samper spent the year on the rack too, accused of taking drug money to fund his 1994 election campaign. Heroin was even found on his presidential jet but Samper claimed it had been planted to smear him.

Washington struck Colombia from its list of countries cooperating in the war on drugs and in July it even revoked Samper's U.S. visa. But he hung onto his job, helped by a sympathetic Colombian congress and an anti-American backlash.
Presidents clung to power elsewhere, with mixed results.
Very popular during their first terms, Peru's Alberto Fujimori and Argentina's Carlos Menem both found the going a lot harder the second time around.
Menem fired his economy minister Domingo Cavallo after a series of spats and suffered the rare indignity of having Congress reject presidential initiatives.
Fujimori also saw his popularity plunge, but that did not deter him from seeking an unprecedented third term.

And if anyone thought eccentric Latin American leaders were a thing of the past, Ecuador's Abdala Bucaram proved them wrong in 1996 by winning election as president. Nicknamed "The Madman," Bucaram made his name in earlier campaigns by wearing a Batman suit. Once sworn in this year, he quickly hit the headlines by releasing a rock n' roll record and throwing banknotes into the crowd during one of his concerts.
He was only living up to his campaign boast that "I do whatever the hell I like."
